claims.text: The untreated eutectic high-entropy alloy has hierarchical dual-phase lamellar colonies.
Dislocation pile-ups at internal phase boundaries produce local stress concentrations in the untreated alloy.
The boundary-associated stress concentrations cause premature microcracking and brittle failure at room temperature.
A trace addition such as Nb or B can be introduced during processing so that it segregates preferentially to the phase interfaces.
Solidification or thermal processing can produce uniform dopant segregation at the phase boundaries.
The trace element will enrich and modify the chemistry and properties of the inter-phase boundaries.
Dopant enrichment will enhance interfacial bonding or enable controlled interface sliding.
Dopant segregation will reduce barriers to dislocation transmission by smoothing the stress gradient across the interface.
Smoothing the interfacial stress gradient will mitigate intense dislocation pile-ups.
Mitigating dislocation pile-ups will reduce local stress concentrations and delay crack nucleation during straining.
Doped interfaces will retain sufficient structural integrity to preserve or increase yield strength and ultimate tensile strength.
Relative to the untreated alloy, the doped alloy will have increased room-temperature tensile ductility.
Relative to the untreated alloy, the doped alloy will maintain or increase strength.
The beneficial effect depends on uniform interfacial segregation of the dopant.
The ductility-strength response will be sensitive to dopant concentration, distribution uniformity, and processing parameters.
Improper segregation or secondary-phase formation may compromise the desired ductility-strength trade-off.
